description: We're building an interactive web tool to explore SPHEREx all-sky images, compare observations over time and spot objects that move or change brightness, possible hints of unknown bodies in the outer Solar System. Code, data and ML are covered; we'd love teammates fascinated by how the universe works who can help us make sense of what the sky is telling us. Bring your curiosity!
summary:
The sky is not still. Stars move, objects change brightness, and distant worlds may reveal themselves through repeated observations.
SPHEREx Sky Blink is an interactive web platform that transforms NASA’s SPHEREx infrared observations into an explorable, time-dependent view of the sky. Using real SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 data, users can navigate the celestial sphere, search astronomical targets or coordinates, compare observations across different dates, and investigate changes through an intuitive blinking interface.
Our platform combines time-based image comparison, infrared wavelength selection, three-dimensional observation stacking, and astronomical data exploration. It includes five recorded target fields and a backend supporting live archive searches, FITS image retrieval, and Gaia DR3 catalogue overlays.
Developed for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, Sky Blink makes repeated infrared observations more accessible and provides a visual foundation for investigating moving and variable astronomical objects. Rather than claiming to have discovered Planet X, our project gives users a way to explore the observational evidence that could contribute to such searches.
details:
The Challenge

NASA’s SPHEREx mission surveys the entire sky in 102 near-infrared spectral bands, repeatedly observing astronomical sources over time. These observations create opportunities to investigate objects that move, brighten, fade, or otherwise change between visits.

However, exploring repeated observations across different dates, wavelengths, and sky positions is not straightforward. Scientific archive data often requires specialized tools and knowledge to retrieve, align, and interpret. Our team addressed the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by developing an interactive system that makes these observations easier to explore and compare.

The Solution: SPHEREx Sky Blink

SPHEREx Sky Blink is a web-based astronomical explorer designed around a simple idea: pick a location in the sky, move through time, and look for change.

·       Explore the sky: navigate an interactive celestial map and zoom into individual fields.

·       Search astronomical coordinates: enter right ascension and declination or select from five predefined targets.

·       Compare observations over time: use a timeline and adjustable playback speed to blink between observations of the same region.

·       Explore infrared wavelengths: select among SPHEREx’s six detector ranges and inspect observations at their recorded wavelengths.

·       Visualize observations in 3D: tilt the field to display observation epochs as spatially separated image layers.

·       Inspect scientific data: view observational metadata, dates, wavelengths, and underlying image-frame information.

The five recorded target fields are Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. They provide examples of astronomical motion or variability for visual investigation.

The Technical Infrastructure

The system combines a Next.js and React frontend with a Python-based astronomical backend. The backend retrieves SPHEREx observations through NASA’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), processes FITS image cutouts, manages cached observations, and supports Gaia DR3 catalogue overlays.

The frontend presents the observations through a custom interactive sky renderer. Users can navigate between the whole sky and detailed fields, select wavelengths, scrub through observation dates, and compare real infrared image frames.

·       Recorded mode: previously retrieved SPHEREx observations for five targets, usable without a live backend.

·       Live mode: backend requests for observations at requested sky positions.

·       Automatic mode: recorded targets plus backend queries for other positions.

The interface reports data limitations when observations are unavailable, archive requests fail, or a field lacks repeated coverage at a comparable wavelength, rather than presenting artificial observations.

Repository link: https://github.com/mrtorture-dev/planet-x-spherex

Scientific Validity

Sky Blink uses actual SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 observations rather than simulated infrared image sequences for its recorded demonstrations. Because observations can differ in wavelength, detector coverage, and date, meaningful comparisons require attention to the underlying data. The platform preserves observational metadata and supports comparisons within selected wavelength ranges. It is an interactive exploration and visualization tool, not an automated Planet X detection pipeline, and does not claim to have discovered a new planet.

Technologies

Frontend: Next.js 14, React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, HTML Canvas.

Backend: Python, astronomical data-processing services, REST APIs, FITS image handling, local caching.

Astronomical resources: NASA SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 via IRSA; ESA Gaia DR3 catalogue integration.

Impact and Future Potential

Sky Blink makes NASA’s infrared observations more approachable for students, researchers, educators, and astronomy enthusiasts. Its contribution is turning complex archival observations into an interactive experience, allowing users to explore astronomical change without first building their own retrieval and visualization pipeline. It also establishes a foundation for future automated moving-object candidate identification, systematic comparisons across repeated surveys, and additional catalogue integration.
